source_text: Nam quod ad ieiunia pertineat, certos dies a deo constitutos opponunt, ut cum in Leuitico praecipit dominus Moysi decimam mensis septimi diem placationis, sancta, inquiens, erit uobis dies, et uexabitis animas uestras, et omnis anima, quae uexata non fuerit in illa die, exterminabitur de populo suo. certe in euangelio illos dies ieiuniis. determinatos putant, in quibus ablatus est sponsus, et hos esse iam solos legitimos ieiuniorum Christianorum abolitis legalibus et propheticis uetustatibus. ubi uolunt enim, adgnoscunt quid sapiat lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem. itaque de cetero indifferenter ieiunandum ex arbitrio, non ex imperio nouae disciplinae, pro temporibus et causis uniuscuiusque; sic et apostolos obseruasse, nullum aliud imponentes iugum certorum et in commune omnibus obeundorum ieiuniorum, proinde nec stationum, quae et ipsae suos quidem dies habeant quartae feriae et sextae, passiue tamen currant, neque sub lege praecepti neque ultra supremam diei, quando et orationes fere hora nona concludat de Petri exemplo, quod Actis refertur. xerophagias uero nouum adfectati officii nomen et proximum ethnicae superstitioni, quales castimoniae Apim, Isidem et Magnam Matrem certorum eduliorum exceptione purificant, cum fides libera in Christo ne Iudaicae quidem legi abstinentiam quorundam ciborum debeat, semel in totum macellum ab apostolo admissa, detestatore eorum qui sicut nubere prohibeant, ita iubeant cibis abstinere a deo conditis. et ideo nos esse iam tunc praenotatos in nouissimis temporibus abscedentes a fide, intendentes spiritibus mundi seductoribus, doctrinis mendaciloquorum inustam habentes conscientiam. quibus, oro te, ignibus? credo, quibus nuptias saepe deducimus et cenas quotidie coquimus? sic et cum Galatis nos quoque percuti aiunt obseruatores dierum et mensium et annorum. iaculantur interea et Esaiam pronuntiasse: non tale ieiunium dominus elegit, id est non abstinentiam cibi, sed opera iustitiae, quae subtexit; et ipsum dominum in euangelio ad omnem circa uictum scrupulositatem compendio respondisse, non his communicari hominem quae in os inferantur, sed quae ex ore proferantur, cum et ipse manducaret et biberet usque in notationem: ecce homo uorator et potator! sic et apostolum docere, quod esca nos deo non commendet, neque abundantes, si edamus, neque deficientes, si non edamus. his et huiusmodi sensibus eo iam subtiliter tendunt, ut unusquisque pronior uentri possit superuacua nec adeo necessaria existimare sublati uel deminuti uel demorati cibi officia, praeponente scilicet deo iustitiae et innocentiae opera. et scimus, quales sint carnalium commodorum suasoriae, quam facile dicatur: opus est de totis praecordiis credam, diligam deum et proximum tamquam me. in his enim duobus praeceptis tota lex pendet et prophetae, non in pulmonum et intestinorum meorum inanitate.
thought_title: Opponents' objections from Scripture and custom
orientation: Tertullian is reporting the objections of the unspiritual Christians against the New Prophecy's fasting practices, quoting their appeals to Scripture and apostolic custom.
pass_a_gloss: For as to what pertains to fasts, they set against us certain days appointed by God, as when in Leviticus the Lord commands Moses the tenth day of the seventh month, a day of propitiation, saying, 'It will be holy for you, and you will afflict your souls, and every soul which will not have been afflicted on that day will be cut off from its people.' Certainly in the gospel they think those days are fixed for fasts in which the bridegroom was taken away, and that these are now the only lawful fasts of Christians, the legal and prophetic old things having been abolished. For where they wish, they recognize what the law and the prophets taste like up to John. And so for the rest one must fast without distinction from choice, not from command of a new discipline, according to the times and causes of each one; and so the apostles observed, imposing no other yoke of fixed fasts to be observed by all in common, and likewise not of station fasts, which also themselves indeed have their own days, the fourth feria and the sixth, but run without distinction, neither under the law of a precept nor beyond the end of the day, since also prayers generally close at the ninth hour from the example of Peter, which is reported in Acts. But dry-food fasts are a new name of an affected duty and next to pagan superstition, such as the chastities which purify Apis, Isis, and the Great Mother by the exception of certain foods, since faith free in Christ owes not even to the Jewish law abstinence from certain foods, the whole meat market having been admitted once for all by the apostle, who detests those who, as they forbid to marry, so command to abstain from foods created by God. And therefore they say we were already then marked out in the last times, departing from faith, attending to spirits of the world, seducers, having a conscience branded by doctrines of liars. By what fires, I ask you? By those, I believe, by which we often lead down weddings and cook dinners daily? So also they say we are struck along with the Galatians as observers of days and months and years. They hurl meanwhile also that Isaiah pronounced: 'The Lord has not chosen such a fast,' that is, not abstinence from food, but works of justice, which he subjoins; and that the Lord himself in the gospel responded to every scrupulousness about food with a summary, that a man is not defiled by those things which are brought into the mouth, but by those things which are brought forth from the mouth, although he himself ate and drank even to the point of being marked: 'Behold a man, a glutton and a drinker!' So also they say the apostle teaches that food does not commend us to God, neither do we abound if we eat, nor do we lack if we do not eat. With these and senses of this kind they now aim so subtly that each one more inclined to the belly can consider the duties of food removed or diminished or delayed as superfluous and not so necessary, God of course preferring works of justice and innocence. And we know what kind are the persuasions of fleshly comforts, how easily it is said: 'I need to believe from all my heart, to love God and my neighbor as myself. For in these two precepts the whole law hangs and the prophets, not in the emptiness of my lungs and intestines.'

pass_b_english: Now as for fasting, they set against us certain days appointed by God. In Leviticus the Lord commands Moses that the tenth day of the seventh month is a day of atonement: "It shall be a holy day for you, and you shall afflict your souls, and every soul that is not afflicted on that day shall be cut off from his people" (Leviticus 16:29). In the gospel they think the days of fasting are fixed as those in which the bridegroom was taken away (Matthew 9:15), and that these are now the only lawful fasts for Christians, since the legal and prophetic old things have been abolished. For they say that where they wish, they recognize what the law and the prophets mean, up to John (Matthew 11:13). And so from then on one must fast without distinction, by choice, not by the command of a new discipline, according to each person's times and causes. They say the apostles observed this too, imposing no other yoke of fixed fasts to be kept by all in common, and likewise no station fasts—which indeed have their own days, the fourth feria and the sixth, but run without distinction, neither under the law of a command nor beyond the end of the day, since prayers generally conclude at the ninth hour, from Peter's example reported in the Acts (Acts 10:9).

Dry-food fasts, however, they call a new name for an affected practice, and next door to pagan superstition—the sort of chastities that purify Apis, Isis, and the Great Mother by excluding certain foods. For faith in Christ is free, and does not owe even the Jewish law abstinence from certain foods, since the whole meat market was once for all admitted by the apostle, who detested those who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods created by God (1 Timothy 4:3). And so they say we were already marked out then, in the last times, departing from the faith, attending to seducing spirits of the world, having a conscience seared by the doctrines of liars (1 Timothy 4:1-2). Branded by what fires, I ask you? By the fires, I suppose, with which we often conduct weddings and cook dinners every day? So too they say that with the Galatians we are struck down as observers of days and months and years (Galatians 4:10).

Meanwhile they hurl at us that Isaiah declared: "The Lord has not chosen such a fast" (Isaiah 58:5)—that is, not abstinence from food, but the works of justice which he goes on to list. And that the Lord himself in the gospel answered every scrupulosity about food with a summary: a man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of his mouth (Matthew 15:11), since he himself ate and drank to the point of being marked: "Behold, a glutton and a drinker!" (Matthew 11:19). So too the apostle teaches that food does not commend us to God: we are no better if we eat, nor worse if we do not eat (1 Corinthians 8:8).

With these and similar arguments they now press so subtly that anyone more inclined to his belly can consider the duties of removing, reducing, or postponing food as superfluous and not really necessary—God, of course, preferring works of justice and innocence. And we know what the persuasions of fleshly comforts are like, how easily it is said: "What I need is to believe with my whole heart, to love God and my neighbor as myself. For on these two commands hang the whole law and the prophets" (Matthew 22:37-40)—not on the emptiness of my lungs and intestines.

fixed: Glossary consistency: The brief's glossary already maps ieiunium to 'fasting', xerophagiae to 'dry-food fasts', and stationes to 'station fasts'; the English uses these consistently, so no edit needed.

Mistranslation 'branded': The source 'inustam habentes conscientiam' (having a conscience branded/seared) reflects 1 Timothy 4:2, where the Greek is 'kekaustēriasmenōn' (seared/cauterized). 'Seared' is the standard rendering and better conveys the sense; edited.

Scripture citation Leviticus 16:29: The source quotes 'decimam mensis septimi diem placationis' (the tenth day of the seventh month, a day of propitiation), which matches Leviticus 23:27 (the Day of Atonement) rather than Leviticus 16:29. However, the brief instructs to use modern numbering where applicable, and the citation is a parenthetical addition. The wording 'tenth day of the seventh month' is from Leviticus 23:27, so the citation should be corrected.

Scripture citation Matthew 11:13: The source 'lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem' (the law and the prophets up to John) is a direct allusion to Matthew 11:13, which in the Vulgate reads 'omnes enim prophetae et lex usque ad Iohannem prophetaverunt'. The English 'mean' is a paraphrase of 'prophesied', but the citation is correct; no edit needed.
Glossary 'unspiritual Christians': The brief's glossary mandates 'unspiritual Christians' for psychici, and the English uses it. No edit needed.

Glossary 'feria': The English uses 'the fourth feria and the sixth', which is a literal rendering of 'quartae feriae et sextae'. The brief's glossary maps stationes to 'station fasts' but does not address 'feria'. The English is clear enough in context; no edit needed.

Speaker marking: The sentence 'For where they wish, they recognize...' is ambiguous. The source 'ubi uolunt enim, adgnoscunt quid sapiat lex et prophetae usque ad Iohannem' is part of the opponents' argument (they recognize the law and prophets only up to John, i.e., selectively). Adding 'they say that' clarifies it is the opponents' view; edited.
